sections.question: Which cost should you include when planning a student budget?
sections.explanation: A student budget should account for course materials as well as tuition, student fees, transportation, and living expenses.

children.text: Checking the library for course materials or choosing used or electronic books may reduce study costs.
Hypothetical example:
Before buying a textbook, Sam checks whether the library has a copy to borrow. If not, Sam compares used and electronic options.

items.question: What living expenses belong in a student budget?

children.text: Consider food, heat, electricity, Internet, tenant’s insurance, and transportation when they apply to you.

items.question: Why should I review my budget each year?

children.text: Tuition and living costs may rise, so an updated budget can reflect current expenses.

sources.title: Managing your budget as a student

sections.question: What is the purpose of a student budget?

options.text: To plan the money you expect to receive and spend
To guarantee that tuition costs will not rise

sections.explanation: A budget helps you understand and manage the money coming in and the costs you expect during your studies.

children.text: A budget can show whether expected income covers tuition, student fees, course materials, living expenses, transportation and other costs.
Hypothetical example:
A student lists expected income and school and living costs. The budget shows a gap, so the student contacts the financial aid office early to discuss available support.

items.question: Which living costs can I include in a budget?

children.text: You can include costs such as food, heat, electricity, Internet, tenant’s insurance and transportation.

items.question: How might I reduce course-material costs?

children.text: Consider used books, electronic versions or borrowing available materials from your school library.

sources.title: Managing your budget as a student

lessons.title: What a Resume Is and How to Choose the Right Format

sections.question: Which resume format emphasizes skills more than specific jobs?
sections.explanation: A functional resume focuses on skills and abilities. A chronological resume focuses on work history, while a hybrid resume combines skills with an experience timeline.

children.text: A format should fit your background, but its content should also fit the position. Reviewing the job description can help you select relevant experience and achievements.
Hypothetical example:

Priya has steady experience in the same field, so she chooses a chronological format. For each application, she reviews the job description and gives more attention to achievements related to that role.

items.question: Can unpaid work appear on a resume?

children.text: Yes. Relevant volunteer or unpaid work can show skills and may be included under work or volunteer experience.

items.question: Should a resume list only job responsibilities?

children.text: No. Highlight relevant achievements and specific examples of what you accomplished instead of only listing duties.

sources.title: How to write a good resume

sections.question: What should you emphasize when tailoring a resume to a position?
sections.explanation: Review the job description, then emphasize relevant experience and achievements that show what you can contribute.

children.text: Choose achievements that match the position. Use clear action verbs and specific, honest results rather than listing duties alone.
Hypothetical example:
A person applying for a retail role selects an achievement about training team members because it demonstrates teamwork and workplace contribution.

items.question: Should every application use identical resume content?

children.text: No. Select experience and achievements related to each position.

items.question: How can an achievement be made clearer?

children.text: Use a specific example, an action verb, and an honest result. Include firm numbers when they are available and accurate.

sources.title: How to write a good resume - Job Bank

sections.question: What should you do if an unexpected email asks you to click a link and enter banking passwords?

options.text: Click the link and check whether the website looks professional
Do not click the link or provide information, and verify the sender
Reply with your password so the sender can confirm your identity

sections.explanation: Phishing messages may lead to fake websites that collect personal information. Do not use their links or share information. Check the sender's identity.

children.text: Caller ID and professional-looking websites can be faked. Verify unexpected requests through an official Government of Canada website or official channel before sharing information or paying.
Hypothetical example:

Lina receives a call claiming to be from IRCC. The caller threatens her and asks for an immediate transfer to a personal bank account. Lina ends the call and checks the claim through the official IRCC website.

items.question: Does a familiar number on caller ID prove that a government call is real?

children.text: No. Scammers can use technology to make a phone number appear real.

items.question: Can anyone guarantee a Canadian job or visa?

children.text: No. No one can guarantee a job or visa, and only immigration officers can decide whether to issue a visa.

sections.question: What should you do when people are waiting in a line?

options.text: Stand very close to the next person

sections.explanation: Waiting your turn respects the people who arrived before you.

children.text: Respectful communication across cultures can help people understand one another and support welcoming communities.
Hypothetical example:
Sam is unsure how to greet a new coworker. Sam politely asks what greeting the coworker prefers.

items.question: What can I do if I am unsure about a social custom?

children.text: Ask politely and pay attention to what others are comfortable with.

items.question: Why is respectful communication useful in a diverse community?

children.text: It can increase cross-cultural understanding and help people feel welcome.

sources.title: Evaluation of the Welcoming Communities Initiative

lessons.title: Urban vs. Suburban vs. Rural: How Location Shapes Your Choice

sections.question: What should someone check when considering a rural home?

options.text: How close it is to the nearest large town
Whether every rural area has the same facilities

sections.explanation: Access to public and private facilities in a rural area can depend on how close the home is to the nearest large town.

children.text: Transportation needs are connected to local access. When comparing communities, consider the location of work, health services, schools, and other facilities.
Hypothetical example:
Sam compares two homes outside a city. One is closer to the nearest large town. Sam checks access to needed facilities and the travel involved before choosing.

items.question: Do all rural communities offer the same access to facilities?

children.text: No. Access can depend on how close the community is to the nearest large town.

items.question: What factors can help when comparing places to live?

children.text: Consider services, weather, cost of living, health services, schools, and where your skills can be used.

sections.question: What should you confirm when checking a private plan's prescription drug coverage?

options.text: Whether your medicines are covered and what your copayment is
Whether every medicine is automatically covered
Whether all pharmacies charge the same retail price

sections.explanation: Coverage can vary by medicine, formulary, pharmacy, and copayment. Ask the plan or check its website for details.

children.text: Before choosing or using a plan, check its prescription list, copayment, annual payment maximum, and any participating-pharmacy rules.
Hypothetical example:
Sam compares two plans. Sam checks whether a regular prescription is listed, what portion Sam must pay, and whether it must be purchased at a participating pharmacy.

items.question: Does every private plan cover every prescription medicine?

children.text: No. A plan may limit coverage to preferred medicines, generic medicines, or purchases from participating pharmacies.

items.question: Where can I check my medicine coverage?

children.text: Ask the plan’s customer service representative or check the plan’s website.

sections.question: When comparing prescription drug coverage, what should you check?

options.text: The copayment, formulary, and annual coverage limit
Only whether the policy number fits on your phone

sections.explanation: These details help show which medicines are covered and what costs or limits may apply.

children.text: A drug formulary is a plan’s list of preferred medicines. A plan may charge more for a medicine outside that list or require members to use participating pharmacies.
Hypothetical example:
Lee compares two plans for a medicine they use. Lee asks whether it is on each formulary, what the copayment is, and whether a particular pharmacy is required.

items.question: Where can I confirm whether my medicine is covered?

children.text: Ask the plan’s customer service representative or check the plan’s website.

items.question: What is an annual coverage limit?

children.text: It is the maximum amount a plan will pay in a year. Check this when comparing plans.

sections.question: Which request is a warning sign of a possible identity scam?

options.text: An unexpected caller asks you to confirm personal information
You contact a government agency directly through its official website
You pause to consider why someone contacted you

sections.explanation: Unexpected requests for personal or financial information are a warning sign. Verify the request through an official channel before responding.

children.text: A scammer may seek personal information by phone, email, or a fake website. Urgency, threats, and requests to click a link are warning signs.
Hypothetical example:

Sam receives an urgent message that appears to come from a government agency. It asks Sam to click a link and enter personal information. Sam does not use the link and contacts the agency directly instead.

items.question: Can a message look official and still be a scam?

children.text: Yes. Scammers may imitate government services or create realistic messages and websites.

items.question: What should I do if I am unsure about a government message?

children.text: Contact the department or agency directly using its official website.

sources.title: Module 7: How to protect yourself from financial fraud
Scams and fraud - Government of Canada

sections.question: Which situation is phishing?

options.text: A realistic-looking email links to a website that asks for account information
A caller leaves a voicemail asking you to confirm personal information
Real and fake information are combined to create a made-up identity

sections.explanation: Phishing uses a legitimate-looking email or website to seek personal or account information. A phone call or voicemail is called vishing.

children.text: Personal information may be obtained through email, phone calls, or fake websites. If a criminal then uses it to access a bank account or open credit in someone else’s name, the information has been misused.
Hypothetical example:
Sam enters account details on a fake website. A criminal later tries to open a credit account in Sam’s name. The fake website collected the information, and the credit application used it.

items.question: What is vishing?

children.text: Vishing is a phone call or voicemail that asks you to provide or confirm personal information.

items.question: What should I do if a message asking for personal information seems uncertain?

children.text: Contact the organization or government department directly instead of using the message’s link or contact details.

sources.title: Module 7: How to protect yourself from financial fraud
Scams and fraud - Government of Canada

sections.question: Which message is a warning sign of a possible financial scam?

options.text: A message demanding immediate payment by gift card
A CRA email saying a document is available in a secure CRA portal

sections.explanation: Urgent demands for payment by gift card are a scam warning sign. The CRA does not demand immediate payment by gift card.

children.text: Urgency, requests for personal or financial information, secrecy, and unusual payment methods are warning signs. Do not use a suspicious link. Contact the organization separately if you are unsure.
Hypothetical example:
Sam receives a text claiming to be from the CRA. It threatens arrest and demands a gift card payment. Sam does not reply or open the link. Sam checks the secure CRA portal separately.

items.question: What are phishing and vishing?

children.text: Phishing uses legitimate-looking emails or websites to seek information. Vishing uses phone calls or voicemail.

items.question: What should I do if I shared financial information with a scammer?

children.text: Notify your financial institution as soon as possible. You can also contact local police and report the incident to the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre.

sources.title: Module 7: How to protect yourself from financial fraud
MP Kit for CRA-related scams and fraud

sections.question: Which message is an example of vishing?

options.text: A voicemail asking you to confirm personal information
An email asking you to enter account information on a website
A job advertisement that includes a company address

sections.explanation: Vishing uses a telephone call or voicemail to request or confirm personal information. Phishing commonly uses email and links.

children.text: Urgency, secrecy, requests for personal information, and demands to send money before receiving a promised benefit are warning signs of fraud.
Hypothetical example:
Sam receives a voicemail promising a job but requiring an administration payment first. Sam recognizes the advance fee as a warning sign and does not pay.

items.question: Can a scam message appear to come from a real organization?

children.text: Yes. Scammers may disguise contact details or create a fake website that looks real.

items.question: What is identity fraud?

children.text: It is the theft of personal or financial information to access bank accounts or open new credit accounts in someone else’s name.

sources.title: Module 7: How to protect yourself from financial fraud

sections.question: Which statement about a permanent resident's mobility rights is correct?

options.text: They may move to another province and pursue a livelihood there, subject to applicable limits.
They may vote in a provincial election after moving.
They are exempt from all provincial laws after moving.

sections.explanation: The Charter protects a permanent resident's right to move to and pursue a livelihood in any province. These rights remain subject to laws of general application and reasonable residency requirements for publicly provided social services.

children.text: Mobility rights are subject to laws that apply generally within a province. Publicly provided social services may also have reasonable residency requirements.
Hypothetical example:
A permanent resident moves to another province for a job. They can pursue work there, but they check that province’s rules before applying for a publicly provided social service.

items.question: Can a permanent resident pursue a livelihood in another province?

children.text: Yes. The Charter protects this right, subject to the stated limits.

items.question: Can publicly provided social services have residency requirements?

children.text: Yes. The Charter allows reasonable residency requirements as a qualification for these services.

sources.title: Annex A: The Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms

sections.question: Which CRA service allows most Canadians to file their current income tax and benefit return online?
sections.explanation: NETFILE allows most Canadians to file their current income tax and benefit return using the Internet.

children.text: Auto-fill My Return can fill in parts of a return when used with EFILE or NETFILE-certified tax software.
Hypothetical example:
Sam uses certified software and chooses Auto-fill My Return. Some tax information is added automatically, and Sam reviews it before filing.

items.question: Can My Account be used after a return is filed?

children.text: Yes. My Account includes a
Change my return
option.

items.question: What can ReFILE do?

children.text: ReFILE can adjust a T1 tax return online through certified EFILE or NETFILE software.

lessons.title: Lesson 2.5: Your Responsibilities & PR Cheat Sheet

sections.question: What proves that you have permanent resident status in Canada?
sections.explanation: A PR card proves that you have permanent resident status in Canada.

children.text: For return to Canada on a commercial vehicle, a permanent resident must show a valid PR card and a passport or refugee travel document. Without a valid PR card, they should apply for a PRTD before returning by commercial vehicle.
Hypothetical example:
Sam is outside Canada and plans to return by airplane, but does not have a valid PR card. Sam applies for a PRTD before returning.

items.question: Does an expired PR card automatically end PR status?

children.text: No. PR status is not lost simply because a PR card expires.

items.question: Must the 730 days in Canada be continuous?

children.text: No. The 730 days during the last five years do not need to be continuous, and some time outside Canada may count.

lessons.title: Cost Comparison: Transit vs. Car Ownership

sections.question: Which expense is part of owning and operating a private vehicle?
sections.explanation: Vehicle ownership costs can include depreciation, fuel, insurance, maintenance, and parking.

children.text: A useful comparison includes the different costs of each option. Car costs can include depreciation, fuel, insurance, maintenance, and parking. Transit costs can include passes or fares.
Hypothetical example:
A person lists their expected car expenses and compares the total with local transit costs. They also consider whether available transit meets their travel needs.

items.question: Which car costs should be included in a comparison?

children.text: Include relevant costs such as depreciation, fuel, insurance, maintenance, and parking.

items.question: Why might two people reach different conclusions?

children.text: Their local transit options and need for a vehicle’s flexibility may differ.

sections.question: Which statement about federal newcomer language training is supported by the source?

options.text: IRCC's Settlement Program funds language training in both official languages.
Every newcomer must complete French training.
Language training is available only in Quebec.

sections.explanation: The source says IRCC's Settlement Program funds flexible, accessible language training in English and French.

children.text: Language training can support newcomers’ social and professional integration. Some federally funded services provide training in either official language.
Hypothetical example:
A French-speaking newcomer living outside Quebec looks for language training that fits their local community and work needs.

items.question: Does federal newcomer language training cover both official languages?

children.text: Yes. The cited IRCC initiative funds training services in English and French.

items.question: Can French-language training be offered outside Quebec?

children.text: Yes. The sources describe providers and courses in provinces outside Quebec.

sources.title: Detailed view of initiative data for: English and/or French Language Training for Newcomers

sections.question: Which celebration is associated with giving thanks and family gatherings?
sections.explanation: The lesson associates Thanksgiving with giving thanks and family gatherings.

children.text: Community events can help people learn about local culture and customs while meeting others.
Hypothetical example:
A newcomer visits a local food festival, speaks with neighbours, and learns about celebrations represented there.

items.question: Where might newcomers in B.C. get help understanding local culture and customs?

children.text: Local community organizations, neighbourhood houses, or libraries may provide newcomer services.

items.question: Can newcomer service workers in B.C. offer support in languages other than English or French?

children.text: They can often support newcomers in their preferred language.

sources.title: Start your life in BC - WelcomeBC

sections.question: Which statement best connects a person's expertise with an audience's needs?

options.text: I have logistics experience and can use it to improve supply chain efficiency.
I am looking for any available opportunity.
I have many interests that I enjoy discussing.

sections.explanation: The correct statement links relevant experience to a result that an employer or client may need.

children.text: A focused UVP identifies a relevant strength and explains how it can help a specific audience.
Hypothetical example:
A bilingual applicant seeking a client-facing role might say, “I use my language skills and cross-cultural communication experience to connect with clients from different backgrounds.”

items.question: Can professional experience from another country be part of a UVP?

children.text: Yes. It can show relevant expertise and an international perspective.

items.question: Where can newcomers look for help with finding a job?

children.text: IRCC states that newcomer services can provide help with job searches and making connections.

sections.question: What is the best way to show that you have a skill during an interview?

options.text: Give a concrete example from relevant experience

sections.explanation: A concrete example helps demonstrate a specific qualification through relevant experience.

children.text: When discussing a skill, connect it to a specific experience. Explain the situation, what you did, and the positive result. The experience may come from work, education, or community involvement if it is relevant.
Hypothetical example:
Asked about teamwork, Sam briefly describes a group project, explains how they organized shared tasks, and states that the team completed the project successfully.

items.question: What skills should I be ready to discuss?

children.text: Prepare relevant job skills and soft skills, such as reliability, teamwork, and learning new things quickly.

items.question: Can I ask the interviewer a question?

children.text: Yes. You can prepare questions about the company or role, such as what tasks are part of a typical day.

sources.title: Recruit newcomers to Canada - Job Bank
Find a job in Canada as a newcomer - Job Bank

sections.question: Which feature should you compare when choosing a credit card?
sections.explanation: Interest rates and fees can affect the cost of using a credit card. Rewards and benefits are also worth comparing.

children.text: When choosing a card, compare its interest rates, fees, rewards, and benefits. Carrying a balance can reduce the value of rewards because interest is usually charged when the balance is not paid in full.
Hypothetical example:
Sam compares two cards. One offers rewards but has an annual fee. The other has no annual fee. Sam considers expected use of the rewards and any interest before choosing.

items.question: What happens if I do not pay my balance in full?

children.text: The card issuer usually charges interest on the unpaid balance. You must still make at least the minimum payment by its due date.

items.question: What should I read before applying for a card?

children.text: Read the terms and conditions, including the interest rates, fees, and other charges. Ask questions about anything you do not understand.

sections.question: Which document may confirm approval for permanent residence?
sections.explanation: A CoPR or eCoPR confirms permanent residence approval. A Biometrics Instruction Letter provides instructions for giving biometrics.

children.text: Accurate identification details matter beyond an immigration application. For example, the CRA says names and dates of birth must exactly match the information linked to a person’s identification number for electronic tax filing.
Hypothetical example:
Sam notices that a job title in a letter differs from the title on a form. Sam checks the source documents and corrects the inconsistency before uploading the files.

items.question: Why should I keep copies of important documents?

children.text: Copies can help if originals are lost. Keep copies in a separate place from the originals.

items.question: What should I do with important documents when travelling to settle in Canada?

children.text: Keep required travel and immigration documents with you rather than packing them in your luggage.

sources.title: Prepare to cross the border to settle in Canada as a newcomer

sections.question: Which document can prove protected person status for a permanent residence application?

options.text: A letter with a positive decision from the Immigration and Refugee Board

sections.explanation: IRCC accepts the letter received with a positive decision from the Immigration and Refugee Board as proof of protected person or Convention refugee status.

children.text: A protected person applying for permanent residence must provide accepted proof of status. This may be a positive decision letter from the Immigration and Refugee Board, a Verification of Status document for a positive Pre-Removal Risk Assessment decision, or a temporary resident permit for a protected temporary resident.
Hypothetical example:
Sam has a positive decision letter from the Immigration and Refugee Board. Sam keeps the original secure and prepares the required copy or upload when completing a permanent residence application.

items.question: Who decides whether someone is a protected person in Canada?

children.text: The Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada and Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada make these decisions.

items.question: Can a protected person apply for permanent residence online or by mail?

children.text: Yes. The application may be submitted online through the Permanent Residence Portal or by mail.

sources.title: Apply for permanent residence as a protected person: How to apply
Applying for Permanent Residence from within Canada: Protected Persons and Convention Refugees (IMM 5205)

sections.question: Which activity is an example of play-based early learning?

options.text: Counting objects in a pretend grocery store

sections.explanation: A pretend grocery store lets children explore counting through play.

children.text: Educators can build activities around children’s curiosity. Books, songs, objects, art, and simple experiments can help children explore language, mathematics, and other ideas.
Hypothetical example:
A child becomes interested in shadows. The educator offers safe objects and invites the group to observe how the shadows change, talk about what they see, and draw pictures.

items.question: Are preschool programs organized the same way across Canada?

children.text: No. Provinces and territories design and deliver their own early childhood education and care policies and programs, so terms and arrangements can vary.

items.question: How can play support early mathematics?

children.text: Children can explore mathematics by counting objects during activities such as pretend grocery-store play.

sources.title: 2023 Recipient biographies – Excellence in Early Childhood Education
sources.publisher: Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada

sources.title: Public Investments in Early Childhood Education and Care in Canada 2013

sections.question: Who has primary responsibility for designing and delivering preschool policies and programs in Canada?
sections.explanation: Provincial and territorial governments have primary responsibility for early childhood education and care policies and programs. Requirements, standards, funding arrangements, and terminology can differ by jurisdiction.

children.text: Program descriptions and rules vary across provinces and territories. Families can compare the program setting, schedule, approach, and local requirements when considering their options.
Hypothetical example:

A family compares a part-day community program with a full-day program at a childcare facility. They review each program’s schedule and learning approach, then check information from their province or territory.

items.question: Are preschool terms and rules the same across Canada?

children.text: No. Definitions, terminology, standards, and funding arrangements vary among provinces and territories.

items.question: Can preschool learning be play-based?

children.text: Yes. The supplied source describes a preschool using play-based and inquiry-based learning with developmentally appropriate activities.

sources.title: Public Investments in Early Childhood Education and Care in Canada 2013
2023 Recipient biographies – Excellence in Early Childhood Education
sources.publisher: Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada

sections.question: Why should families check information for their own province or territory?

options.text: Early childhood education and care policies and programs vary by jurisdiction.
One province sets preschool rules for all of Canada.
Every preschool has the same program and requirements.

sections.explanation: Provincial and territorial governments have primary responsibility for early childhood education and care policies and programs.

children.text: Preschool terminology, standards, funding arrangements, and program formats can differ among provinces and territories. Families should use information for their own jurisdiction and ask the program directly about its process.
Hypothetical example:
A family finds a preschool they like. They check their provincial or territorial government website for local program information, then contact the preschool to ask what documents it requires.

items.question: Are preschool programs organized the same way across Canada?

children.text: No. Definitions, terminology, standards, and funding arrangements can vary among provinces and territories.

items.question: Can preschool be offered for part of the day?

children.text: Yes. The source describes nursery schools and preschools as part-day programs in some jurisdictions.

sources.title: Public Investments in Early Childhood Education and Care in Canada 2013

sections.question: Which activity can help children explore early literacy skills through play?
sections.explanation: Stories and songs can introduce literacy skills in a playful, age-appropriate way.

children.text: Educators can build activities around children’s curiosity. They may add books, materials, or simple experiments that help children investigate an idea.
Hypothetical example:
A child wonders how shadows change. The educator provides a light and safe objects so the group can explore reflections and shadows together.

items.question: Can play support learning?

children.text: Yes. Play-based activities can introduce literacy, mathematics, creativity, and social skills.

items.question: How can families take part in a preschool community?

children.text: Some programs invite families to volunteer, join activities or field trips, and discuss their children’s interests with educators.

sources.title: 2023 Recipient biographies – Excellence in Early Childhood Education
sources.publisher: Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada

sections.question: Who has primary responsibility for designing and delivering preschool policies and programs in Canada?
sections.explanation: Provincial and territorial governments have primary responsibility for early childhood education and care. Requirements, standards, funding arrangements, and terminology can vary by jurisdiction.

children.text: Play-based activities can build several skills together. For example, stories and songs can support literacy, while pretend-store activities can introduce counting.
Hypothetical example:
A child becomes interested in grocery stores. An educator provides pretend food and invites the child to count the items while talking and cooperating with classmates.

items.question: Are preschool rules the same across Canada?

children.text: No. Provinces and territories design and deliver their own programs, so requirements and terminology can differ.

items.question: How can families take part in preschool learning?

children.text: Families can communicate with educators, share relevant information about their child, ask questions, and participate in activities when invited.

sources.publisher: Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada

sections.question: What should you do if you do not understand an interview question?

options.text: Ask the interviewer to explain it

sections.explanation: Asking for clarification helps you understand the question and give an appropriate answer.

children.text: Before an interview, identify accomplishments that relate to the position. Be ready to explain what you did, how you did it, and the result.
Hypothetical example:
Priya is interviewing for a customer service role. She prepares a short example of how she listened to a customer, addressed the concern, and achieved a positive result.

items.question: What can I ask when an interview is scheduled?

children.text: You can ask whether there will be a test and how many people will attend.

items.question: What materials can I bring to an in-person interview?

children.text: You can bring copies of your résumé and reference list, along with paper and a pen.

sources.title: Preparing for an interview - Job Bank
Stand out to employers and land your dream job - Job Bank

sections.question: Which statement about BC's Medical Services Plan is correct?

options.text: It covers medically necessary hospital and doctor services for BC residents.
It is a private plan offered only by employers.
It covers every prescription drug for every Canadian resident.

sections.explanation: MSP is BC's provincial health insurance program. It covers medically necessary hospital and doctor services for BC residents.

children.text: In BC, Health Insurance BC administers both MSP and PharmaCare. MSP covers medically necessary hospital and doctor services. PharmaCare programs may cover eligible prescription drugs and designated medical supplies.
Hypothetical example:
Sam uses MSP for a medically necessary doctor visit. Sam then checks whether an eligible prescription is covered through a PharmaCare program.

items.question: Who administers MSP and PharmaCare in BC?

children.text: Health Insurance BC administers both programs on behalf of the BC government.

items.question: Does MSP have the same role as PharmaCare?

children.text: No. MSP covers medically necessary hospital and doctor services, while PharmaCare programs cover eligible prescription drugs and designated medical supplies.

sections.question: Which action can help build a stronger and more inclusive community?
sections.explanation: Volunteering with schools or local charities is one way to participate actively in the community.

children.text: People can strengthen local connections by helping neighbours, attending community events, or joining local groups.
Hypothetical example:
Sam attends a neighbourhood event and asks a community group how to support a future local activity.

items.question: What are some ways to participate in a community?

children.text: You can attend local events, help neighbours, volunteer, or join a community group.

items.question: How can community organizations help people connect?

children.text: They can offer community-building activities, resources, and local programs.

sections.question: Which feature distinguishes a credit union from a bank?

options.text: Its members participate in its governance
It must operate without online services

sections.explanation: A credit union is a member-owned financial cooperative, and its members actively participate in its governance.

children.text: Compare the products you need, fees, interest rates, access options, and consumer protection. A single institution may be convenient, but another may offer better terms for a particular service.
Hypothetical example:
Sam wants convenient branch access for daily banking and useful budgeting features. Sam compares branch locations, account fees, and digital tools before choosing an institution.

items.question: Do all financial institutions offer the same products?

children.text: No. Some offer many products, while others specialize in particular services.

items.question: Why should I check who regulates an institution?

children.text: The regulator affects the consumer protections available, including complaint processes and deposit protection.

sections.question: Which service can help connect people in BC with a family doctor or nurse practitioner in their community?
sections.explanation: The Health Connect Registry helps connect people and families in BC with a family doctor or nurse practitioner in their community.

children.text: Primary care may be provided by a family doctor or nurse practitioner. In a Primary Care Network, providers work as a team to coordinate care.
Hypothetical example:
Sam needs a routine checkup and help renewing a prescription. Sam contacts a local primary care clinic to ask about these services.

items.question: Can a nurse practitioner provide primary care in BC?

children.text: Yes. Primary care is usually delivered by family doctors or nurse practitioners.

items.question: What kind of care does a walk-in clinic provide?

children.text: Walk-in clinics provide non-urgent medical care, including assessment and treatment for minor illnesses and injuries.

sections.question: Which service provides same-day care for an urgent but non-emergency health concern?

options.text: An Urgent and Primary Care Centre

sections.explanation: UPCCs provide same-day primary care for urgent, non-life-threatening illnesses and injuries.

children.text: The urgency of a health concern helps distinguish between these services. Walk-in clinics offer non-urgent care, while UPCCs address urgent concerns that are not life-threatening.
Hypothetical example:
Sam has a sprain that needs prompt medical attention but is not life-threatening. Sam looks for a nearby UPCC and checks its hours.

items.question: Do walk-in clinics always require an appointment?

children.text: Usually not. Some clinics also offer same-day appointments.

items.question: Are all UPCCs open at the same times?

children.text: No. Many open during evenings, weekends, and statutory holidays, but hours vary by clinic.

sections.question: Which situation is best suited to a B.C. Urgent and Primary Care Centre rather than emergency care?

options.text: A non-life-threatening injury that needs prompt medical attention

sections.explanation: Urgent and Primary Care Centres provide urgent, non-emergency care. Life-threatening emergencies require emergency care.

children.text: In B.C., Urgent and Primary Care Centres provide same-day care for illnesses or injuries that need prompt attention but are not life-threatening.
Hypothetical example:
Sam has a minor sprain that needs prompt assessment but is not life-threatening. Sam considers an Urgent and Primary Care Centre instead of emergency care.

items.question: What care does an Urgent and Primary Care Centre provide?

children.text: It provides same-day, urgent, non-emergency primary health care in B.C.

items.question: What are examples of concerns treated there?

children.text: Examples include minor injuries, sprains, strains, infections, cuts, wounds, and skin conditions.

sections.question: Which service is listed as part of primary care in B.C.?
sections.explanation: HealthLink BC lists prescription renewal as an example of primary care.

children.text: Prescription renewal can be part of primary care. Primary care is usually provided by family doctors or nurse practitioners.
Hypothetical example:
Sam needs a prescription renewed. Sam contacts a primary care provider to ask about renewal.

items.question: Who usually provides primary care in B.C.?

children.text: Family doctors or nurse practitioners usually provide it.

items.question: Can HealthLink BC connect callers with a pharmacist?

children.text: Yes. In B.C., callers can use 8-1-1 to speak with a pharmacist.

sections.question: Which statement about Fair PharmaCare is correct?

options.text: Coverage is based on family income.

sections.explanation: Fair PharmaCare coverage is based on family income. Not every medication is covered, and people with private health insurance may still receive help.

children.text: PharmaCare processes coverage at the pharmacy counter when a prescription is dispensed, so the person does not submit receipts.
Hypothetical example:
Sam is registered for Fair PharmaCare and fills an eligible prescription at a participating pharmacy. The pharmacy processes any available PharmaCare coverage at the counter.

items.question: Can someone with private health insurance register?

children.text: Yes. They may still receive help with costs from Fair PharmaCare.

items.question: Does Fair PharmaCare cover every medication?

children.text: No. The provincial drug list shows which medications and plans have coverage. Some coverage requires a request from a prescriber.

sources.title: BC PharmaCare: Get help paying for medications and medical supplies

sections.question: In Metro Vancouver, what should you do to avoid charging another payment card by mistake?

options.text: Remove the card you want to tap from your wallet
Tap your whole wallet on the reader
Use two payment cards at the same time

sections.explanation: TransLink advises removing the card from your wallet so the reader does not unintentionally charge another payment card.

children.text: In Metro Vancouver, a Compass Card can hold stored value or a prepaid pass. Contactless debit, credit, and mobile wallets can also be tapped for one adult traveller.
Hypothetical example:
Sam plans to take one Metro Vancouver bus trip. Sam chooses a contactless debit card, removes it from the wallet, and taps it on the reader.

items.question: Can two riders use one Compass Card for the same journey?

children.text: No. Each rider needs a separate form of payment.

items.question: What happens when stored value is used on a Compass Card?

children.text: The fare is automatically deducted from the card’s balance.

sections.question: Which Compass Card option automatically deducts the fare from the card balance?
sections.explanation: When Stored Value is used, the fare is deducted from the card balance. Monthly Pass and DayPass riders tap to validate prepaid travel.

children.text: A reloadable Compass Card can hold Stored Value or prepaid passes. The suitable choice depends on how a person plans to travel in Metro Vancouver.
Hypothetical example:
Sam expects to make several trips in one day. Sam checks whether a DayPass suits those plans before loading a fare product.

items.question: Can one Compass Card pay for two riders on the same journey?

children.text: No. Each rider needs a separate form of payment.

items.question: Who decides whether a student is eligible for U-Pass BC?

children.text: The student’s post-secondary institution determines eligibility.

sections.question: Which option can help someone meet people, contribute to the community, and gain experience?

options.text: Waiting for a club to contact you

sections.explanation: Volunteering can help people make connections, contribute to their community, and gain work experience or volunteer hours.

children.text: A short event role can be a practical way to explore volunteering before considering a larger commitment.
Hypothetical example:
A student who does not want to join a club volunteers at an open house. They meet other volunteers and gain experience helping at a campus event.

items.question: Can volunteering help me connect with other people?

children.text: Yes. Volunteering can help you meet people while contributing to your community.

items.question: Where else can I look for community activities?

children.text: Community centres, recreation centres, and libraries may offer activities and services. Check your city or town website for local information.

sources.title: Settling in Canada: Connecting with your community

lessons.title: Recognizing Mental Health & Understanding the Basics

sections.question: Which statement about stress is accurate?

options.text: Stress is a normal response to changes and daily challenges.
Stress always means a person has a mental illness.

sections.explanation: Stress can be a normal response to change and challenges. Constant stress, however, can create health problems.

children.text: Changes in thinking, mood, or behaviour may be linked to significant distress or difficulty functioning. Stress can also affect focus and wellbeing.
Hypothetical example:
Priya notices that ongoing financial pressure is making it harder to focus at work. She recognizes that the stress is affecting her daily functioning.

items.question: Can stress be a normal response?

children.text: Yes. Stress is a normal response to changes and challenges, although constant stress can cause health problems.

items.question: What is stigma related to mental health?

children.text: Stigma occurs when people judge someone because of a mental health problem, often because they do not understand it or believe inaccurate ideas.

sections.question: Which statement about stress is accurate?

options.text: Stress is a normal response to changes and daily challenges.
Stress always means a person has a mental illness.
Stress affects everyone in exactly the same way.

sections.explanation: Stress can be a normal response to change and challenges. Constant stress, however, can cause health problems.

children.text: Changes in mood, thinking, or behaviour may become a mental illness when they are linked with significant distress and difficulty functioning.
Hypothetical example:
After a major change, Lee feels stressed and takes breaks when it becomes hard to focus. This recognizes that symptoms can affect concentration.

items.question: Is mild or moderate anxiety always a mental illness?

children.text: No. Mild to moderate anxiety is common.

items.question: Can mental health problems be treated?

children.text: Yes. Mental health problems are medical problems that can be treated.

sections.question: Which description best matches depression?

options.text: Persistent sadness, low energy, or loss of interest
A normal response to a brief change

sections.explanation: Depression can involve persistent sadness, reduced energy, and loss of interest in activities previously enjoyed.

children.text: Changes in mood, thinking, or behaviour may become a mental health concern when they cause significant distress or make daily functioning harder.
Hypothetical example:
Sam has stopped enjoying familiar activities, has less energy, and withdraws from friends. These signs fit the description of depression and should not be dismissed as a personal fault.

items.question: Is all anxiety severe?

children.text: No. Mild to moderate anxiety is common. Severe anxiety may involve helplessness, confusion, or extreme worry that is out of proportion to its cause.

items.question: When can stress become harmful?

children.text: Stress is a normal response to change and daily challenges, but constant stress can create health problems.

sections.question: Which situation most clearly suggests that seeking support may be useful?

options.text: Changes are affecting the person's daily life

sections.explanation: Signs that persist or affect daily life may indicate that it is time to seek support.

children.text: Changes in thinking, mood, or behaviour may be linked with significant distress or difficulty functioning. Looking at their effect on everyday activities can help someone recognize when support may be useful.
Hypothetical example:
Alex has trouble focusing and begins missing activities they usually value. Alex notices that these changes are affecting daily life and decides to seek support.

items.question: Can mental health difficulties affect concentration?

children.text: Yes. Symptoms may make it harder to focus for a long time.

items.question: Are mental health problems a person's fault?

children.text: No. Mental health problems are medical problems that can be treated.

sections.question: Which option is an example of community or peer support?
sections.explanation: Support groups are a form of community or peer support. Mindfulness is a self-help strategy, while a doctor's assessment is medical support.

children.text: Different sources of support can be used together. If someone is struggling but not in immediate danger, they can contact a trusted person and a health professional to discuss next steps.
Hypothetical example:
Sam’s stress continues despite improving sleep and routines. Sam talks with a trusted friend and contacts a counsellor for additional support.

items.question: Can I use more than one type of support?

children.text: Yes. For example, someone may use self-help strategies while also speaking with a counsellor, doctor, or support group.

items.question: Where can I look for community support?

children.text: Local or online groups, community organizations, and newcomer organizations may offer support. A doctor, counsellor, or trusted teacher may also help you find options.

sources.title: Getting Help During a Mental Health Crisis

sections.question: If someone in BC thinks they could be in immediate danger during a mental health crisis, what should they do?

options.text: Call 9-1-1 or go to an emergency room
Wait for a routine school appointment
Search only for an online group

sections.explanation: HealthLink BC says to call 9-1-1 or go to an emergency room when you think you could be in danger.

children.text: The right starting point depends on the situation. A doctor or mental health professional can help identify next steps. In a crisis, immediate help may be needed.
Hypothetical example:
Alex is struggling but is not in immediate danger. Alex contacts a trusted relative and calls a health professional to discuss next steps.

items.question: Who can help me decide what to do next?

children.text: A doctor, nurse advice line, or mental health professional can help you consider next steps.

items.question: What should I do if I may be in immediate danger?

children.text: Call 9-1-1 or go to an emergency room and say that you are having a mental health crisis.

sources.title: Getting Help During a Mental Health Crisis

sections.question: What should you do if you think you may need emergency care during a mental health crisis?

options.text: Call 9-1-1 or go to an emergency room
Use only a general resource directory

sections.explanation: HealthLink BC says to call 9-1-1 or go to an emergency room if you think you could be in danger or may need emergency care.

children.text: The right source of support depends on the situation. Emergency help is appropriate when there is immediate danger. When someone is struggling but not in danger, they can contact a trusted person, crisis line, doctor, or mental health professional.
Hypothetical example:
Sam is distressed but says they are not in immediate danger. Sam calls a trusted relative and asks them to stay nearby while Sam contacts a crisis line for support.

items.question: How can I prepare before a possible crisis?

children.text: Identify trusted people and professional supports you could contact. Consider saving crisis numbers in your phone.

items.question: Who can help me decide what to do next?

children.text: A doctor, nurse advice line, or mental health professional can help you consider next steps.

sources.title: Getting Help During a Mental Health Crisis

sections.question: What should you do if you think you could be in immediate danger?

options.text: Call 911 or go to an emergency room
Wait to see whether the danger passes

sections.explanation: Get emergency help right away if you think you could be in danger. Call 911 or go to an emergency room.

children.text: If you are struggling but not in immediate danger, you can contact a trusted person, crisis hotline, doctor, nurse advice line, or mental health professional.
Hypothetical example:
Lee feels distressed but is not in immediate danger. Lee calls a trusted friend and asks them to stay nearby while Lee contacts a crisis hotline for support.

items.question: What if I am unsure whether my situation is an emergency?

children.text: Get emergency help. Call 911 or go to an emergency room.

items.question: Who can help when I am struggling but not in immediate danger?

children.text: You can contact a trusted friend or relative, a crisis hotline, your doctor, a nurse advice line, or a mental health professional.

sources.title: Getting Help During a Mental Health Crisis

sections.question: If someone is struggling but is not in immediate danger, what is an appropriate first step?

options.text: Contact a trusted person or a health professional
Wait until the situation becomes an emergency

sections.explanation: A trusted person, doctor, nurse advice line, or mental health professional can offer support and help identify next steps.

children.text: A first step can be contacting someone you trust or a health professional. They can listen and help you consider what to do next.
Hypothetical example:
Amir feels overwhelmed but is not in immediate danger. He tells a trusted friend how he feels and contacts a health professional for guidance.

items.question: Who can I contact if I do not know where to start?

children.text: You can contact a trusted person, doctor, nurse advice line, therapist, or other counsellor.

items.question: What should I do if I think I could hurt myself or someone else?

children.text: Get emergency help right away. Call 9-1-1 or go to an emergency room and say that you are having a mental health crisis.

sources.title: Getting Help During a Mental Health Crisis

sections.question: If someone is struggling but is not in immediate danger, what is one appropriate step?

options.text: Contact a trusted friend, relative, or health professional
Keep the situation secret from everyone
Rely only on personal stories for support

sections.explanation: Personal stories may help someone feel understood, but direct support can come from a trusted person or health professional.

children.text: Shared experiences can offer comfort and perspective. They can also encourage someone to identify people or professionals they could contact for direct support.
Hypothetical example:
Sam reads an online story that feels familiar. Sam then writes down a trusted friend’s name and a health professional to contact if support is needed.

items.question: Where can I look for people with similar experiences?

children.text: Local groups, online groups, and community organizations may help people connect with others who understand their experiences.

items.question: Are personal stories a replacement for direct help during a crisis?

children.text: No. If there is possible danger, seek emergency help. If there is no immediate danger, contact a trusted person or health professional.

sources.title: Getting Help During a Mental Health Crisis

sections.question: What does work-life balance involve?

options.text: Using sustainable time and energy for work and personal commitments
Giving all available time and energy to work
Avoiding all personal commitments during the workweek

sections.explanation: Work-life balance means devoting a sustainable amount of time and energy to both work and personal commitments.

children.text: Balance and rest can help prevent stress and burnout. They can also support creativity and new ideas.
Hypothetical example:
After completing the day’s work, an employee rests and spends time on a personal commitment. They return to work ready to focus.

items.question: Can flexible schedules or telework support work-life balance?

children.text: Yes. They are examples of alternative work arrangements used by DND/CAF, although arrangements depend on the workplace.

items.question: Why is rest part of work-life balance?

children.text: Rest can help prevent stress and burnout and foster creativity and new ideas.

sections.question: Where is a U-Pass BC loaded for travel?
sections.explanation: Students must load their U-Pass BC onto an Adult Compass Card and request it each month before travelling.

children.text: Linking a Compass Card is not the final step. An eligible student must also request the U-Pass BC each month before travelling.
Hypothetical example:
Sam has already linked an Adult Compass Card. Before taking transit in a new month, Sam signs in and requests that month’s U-Pass BC.

items.question: Can I use U-Pass BC on transit across British Columbia?

children.text: No. It is valid on TransLink services in Metro Vancouver.

items.question: Who decides whether a student is eligible?

children.text: Each participating post-secondary institution determines student eligibility using the program criteria. Ask your institution’s U-Pass BC representative about your status.

sections.question: Which item is listed as a requirement for an adult citizenship grant?

options.text: Giving up permanent resident status before applying

sections.explanation: Adult grant requirements include taking the Oath of Citizenship. They also include filing taxes if required and not being prohibited.

children.text: Permanent residents who apply and meet the requirements of the Citizenship Act are granted citizenship. Adult requirements include filing taxes if required and taking the Oath of Citizenship.
Hypothetical example:
Sam confirms that the applicable requirements are met, submits a citizenship application, and later takes the Oath of Citizenship as part of becoming a citizen.

items.question: Who is responsible for Canadian citizenship?

children.text: Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada is responsible for Canadian citizenship, which is governed by the Citizenship Act.

items.question: What topics does the citizenship study guide cover?

children.text: It covers Canada’s history, government, symbols, and regions.

lessons.title: Protecting Your Finances and Taking Action

sections.question: A text from an unknown sender asks you to open a link and enter your banking password. What should you do?

options.text: Open the link and check whether the page looks official
Do not open the link or provide information, and verify the sender
Reply with your password so the sender can confirm your identity

sections.explanation: Phishing messages may lead to websites that request banking information. Do not click their links or provide personal information. Check who sent the message.

children.text: Caller ID can be faked, so a familiar number does not prove that a message or call is genuine.
Hypothetical example:
Sam receives a text that appears to come from a government agency and asks for banking information. Sam does not use the link and checks the sender’s identity through an official channel.

items.question: Does a familiar number on caller ID prove that a caller is genuine?

children.text: No. Scammers can use technology to make a number appear real.

items.question: Should I let an unexpected caller access my computer to remove a virus?

children.text: No. Never give computer access to someone you did not contact for help.

sections.question: A message from a stranger asks you to open a link and enter your banking password. What should you do?

options.text: Open the link and check whether it looks real
Do not open the link or provide information
Reply with a question about the message

sections.explanation: Phishing messages may lead to websites that request banking details. Do not click their links or share personal information.

children.text: Caller ID is not proof that a caller is legitimate because scammers can make a phone number appear real.
Hypothetical example:
A caller claims to be a government official and demands immediate payment. Sam does not provide a file number or payment information and ends the call.

items.question: Can a caller's displayed phone number prove who is calling?

children.text: No. Scammers can use technology to make a phone number appear real.

items.question: Should I let an unexpected caller access my computer to remove a virus?

children.text: No. Never give computer access to someone you did not contact for help.

sections.question: What should you do if an unexpected message asks you to follow a link and enter banking passwords?

options.text: Click the link and check whether it looks official
Do not click the link or provide information
Reply with your password to confirm your identity

sections.explanation: Unexpected links may lead to phishing websites. Do not click them or share personal information. Check who sent the message.

children.text: Caller ID can be faked, so a familiar-looking number does not prove that a caller is legitimate. Do not share private information unless you know who is receiving it.
Hypothetical example:
Priya receives an unexpected call asking for her immigration file number. Although the number looks official, she does not provide it because caller ID can be faked.

items.question: Can caller ID prove that a government caller is legitimate?

children.text: No. Scammers can use technology to make a phone number appear real.

items.question: Should I give remote computer access to an unexpected caller offering virus help?

children.text: No. Never give computer access to someone you did not contact for help.

sections.question: Which request is most likely to produce focused feedback?

options.text: Can you review how I describe my experience on my resume?
Can you tell me everything I should improve?
Can you find someone else to write my resume?

sections.explanation: A specific request tells the reviewer exactly what to examine.

children.text: Focused feedback can help you identify one clear improvement. Choose someone whose experience fits the task, then consider how to apply the suggestion.
Hypothetical example:
Lina asks a settlement professional to review how clearly her resume presents her work experience. After receiving one suggestion, she revises that section and thanks the reviewer.

items.question: Who could I ask for job-search feedback?

children.text: You could ask a mentor, peer, supervisor, or settlement professional. Canada.ca says settlement professionals can help newcomers adjust and provides job-search resources.

items.question: What should I do after receiving feedback?

children.text: Consider the suggestion, make useful changes, and thank the person for their time.

sections.question: Which option provides same-day care in B.C. for an urgent health concern that is not an emergency?

options.text: An Urgent and Primary Care Centre
A hospital emergency room for every concern

sections.explanation: Urgent and Primary Care Centres provide same-day care for urgent, non-emergency concerns. Emergency rooms are for potentially life-threatening symptoms or major accidents.

children.text: In B.C., a family doctor, care provider, or walk-in clinic may help with a non-emergency concern. A UPCC is another option when urgent, same-day, non-emergency care is needed.
Hypothetical example:
Sam has a minor sprain that needs prompt attention but is not an emergency. Sam checks whether a nearby UPCC can provide same-day care.

items.question: What should I do if I am unsure whether a concern is an emergency?

children.text: In B.C., call HealthLink BC at 8-1-1 for advice.

items.question: Are UPCC hours the same at every clinic?

children.text: No. Actual hours vary by clinic, so check the specific location.

sources.title: When to visit the emergency room

sections.question: In British Columbia, which option is intended for urgent, same-day care that is not an emergency?

options.text: An Urgent and Primary Care Centre

sections.explanation: UPCCs provide urgent, same-day, non-emergency care. Emergency rooms and 911 are for life-threatening illnesses or injuries.

children.text: In British Columbia, a UPCC can help with an urgent concern that does not require hospital emergency care. If you are unsure whether a concern is an emergency, call 8-1-1 for advice.
Hypothetical example:
Sam has a minor sprain that needs prompt attention but is not life-threatening. Sam checks for a nearby UPCC rather than going to the emergency room.

items.question: What should I do for a potentially life-threatening symptom?

children.text: Call 9-1-1 or go to the nearest emergency room right away.

items.question: Are all UPCCs open at the same times?

children.text: No. Hours vary by clinic, so check the specific location.

sources.title: When to visit the emergency room

sections.question: Which tool can a person in B.C. call if they are unsure whether a health concern is an emergency?
sections.explanation: HealthLink BC advises people in B.C. to call 8-1-1 if they are unsure whether a health concern is an emergency.

children.text: HealthLink BC’s 8-1-1 service can provide health information and connect callers with a health professional. Urgent and Primary Care Centres provide same-day care for urgent concerns that are not emergencies.
Hypothetical example:
A person in B.C. has a non-emergency health concern and is unsure where to seek care. They call 8-1-1 for guidance.

items.question: What can 8-1-1 help with in B.C.?

children.text: A navigator can guide callers to reliable health information or connect them with a health professional.

items.question: What is an Urgent and Primary Care Centre?

children.text: It is an alternative to a hospital emergency department for same-day, urgent health concerns that are not emergencies.

sources.title: When to visit the emergency room

sections.question: Which statement about an in-Canada H&C application is correct?

options.text: It is assessed case by case and involves discretionary decision-making.
It is decided through a points ranking.
It is a regular pathway for every person in Canada.

sections.explanation: IRCC states that H&C applications are assessed case by case, involve highly discretionary decision-making, and are not intended to be a regular pathway.

children.text: An H&C decision considers the individual circumstances presented in an application. Evidence helps explain those circumstances.
Hypothetical example:

A person in Canada describes their family and community ties and provides documents supporting those details. The decision-maker reviews the person’s particular circumstances rather than assigning points.

items.question: Is H&C intended to be a regular immigration pathway?

children.text: No. IRCC says it is not intended to be a regular pathway.

items.question: Does submitting an H&C request guarantee permanent residence?

children.text: No. Each application is assessed individually, and decision-making is highly discretionary.

sources.title: CIMM – Humanitarian and Compassionate and Other Immigration – March 23, 2026
CIMM - Humanitarian and Compassionate and Other Immigration - December 4, 2025

sections.question: What should you do if an interview question is unclear?

options.text: Ask the interviewer to explain it

sections.explanation: Asking for clarification helps you understand the question and give a relevant answer.

children.text: Before an interview, identify accomplishments that relate to the position. Be ready to explain what you did, how you did it, and the result.
Hypothetical example:
Sam is interviewing for a customer service role. Sam prepares a short story about resolving a customer concern and explains the steps taken and the result.

items.question: What can I ask when an interview is scheduled?

children.text: You can ask whether the process includes a test and how many people will attend the interview.

items.question: How can company research help me prepare?

children.text: It can help you understand the role, show genuine interest, and prepare informed questions for the interviewer.

sources.title: Preparing for an interview - Job Bank
Stand out to employers and land your dream job - Job Bank

sections.question: Which mortgage choice can lower regular payments but increase total interest costs?

options.text: Paying the mortgage balance at the end of the term

sections.explanation: A longer amortization spreads repayment over more time. Regular payments are lower, but more interest is paid overall.

children.text: The mortgage term is how long the current contract lasts. The amortization period is the estimated time needed to repay the mortgage. Both can affect payments, interest costs, and overall costs.
Hypothetical example:
A buyer compares two mortgages with different amortization periods. The longer option has lower regular payments, but the buyer notices that it would cost more interest over time.

items.question: What happens when a mortgage term ends?

children.text: You generally need to renew the mortgage unless you pay the remaining balance.

items.question: Why should I compare amortization periods?

children.text: A longer amortization can reduce regular payments while increasing the total interest paid.

sections.question: How does a longer amortization period generally affect a mortgage?

options.text: It lowers regular payments but increases total interest costs.
It raises regular payments and reduces total interest costs.
It removes the need to renew the mortgage.

sections.explanation: Taking longer to repay a mortgage generally lowers regular payments, but more interest is paid over time.

children.text: A mortgage term is how long the current contract applies. Amortization is the estimated time needed to repay the mortgage. Both can affect payments and overall costs.
Hypothetical example:
At renewal, Sam compares available terms and interest rates. Sam also considers whether a shorter amortization would fit the household budget and reduce interest costs over time.

items.question: Does a mortgage term cover the full repayment period?

children.text: Not usually. A borrower will likely need several terms to repay a mortgage unless the balance is paid at the end of a term.

items.question: Why compare interest rates at renewal?

children.text: The interest rate affects mortgage payments and interest costs. Borrowers may be able to negotiate with a lender or mortgage broker.

sections.question: Where can an SCA first-year student look for posted advising schedules?
sections.explanation: The SFU School for the Contemporary Arts page says advising schedules will be posted on Advisor Link.

children.text: Official advising can complement course-planning tools when a student has questions about registration.
Hypothetical example:
An SCA first-year student has a registration question. They check Advisor Link for an advising session instead of relying only on student reviews or chats.

items.question: Can advising help with course-registration questions?

children.text: Yes. The SCA source directs students with course-registration questions to planning and advising support.

items.question: Where are SCA advising schedules posted?

children.text: They are posted on Advisor Link.

sources.title: SCA Fall 2026 Course Planning 101 (First Year Students)

sections.question: Where should a student look for an SCA advising schedule mentioned by the official source?
sections.explanation: The official SCA page says advising schedules will be posted on Advisor Link.

children.text: Official faculty pages can provide program-specific course-planning information and direct students to advising support.
Hypothetical example:
A first-year SCA student has a registration question. They check the official SCA page, follow its Advisor Link, and contact the listed SCA New Student Advisor if they still need help.

items.question: Where does the SCA source direct students to find advising schedules?

children.text: It directs students to Advisor Link.

items.question: What can an SCA student do if the official page does not answer their question?

children.text: They can contact the SCA New Student Advisor listed on the page.

sources.title: SCA Fall 2026 Course Planning 101 (First Year Students)
